newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INTERVIEW - Novus says Oman gas field a star.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Novus says Oman gas field a star.

text.p: Novus Petroleum Ltd, which has seen its stock trade at record levels this week, said on Wednesday that its part-owned Bukha gas field in Oman was offering the best returns of all the company's assets.

"The Bukha asset has probably been our best performing asset in terms of return on investment, about a 20 percent plus project for us," Novus manager of corporate research, Mike Sandy, said in an interview.
Novus this year expects to produce about 27,500 barrels of oil equivalent a day from fields in Oman, Australia and Indonesia and will spend about US$22 million on exploration.

Novus shares have gained 27 cents to A$3.72 since Tuesday, when the company announced it was increasing its stake in the Bukha project to 40 percent from 10 by buying the 30 percent stake held by Canada-based International Petroleum Corp's for US$26.5 million.

The purchase takes in the producing Bukha gas-condensate field as well as part of the West Bukha/Henjam field, which is located mostly in Iranian waters. In addition there is exploration potential associated with the Bukha field.

Sandy said the Bukha project was unique in its structure in that the field's production of 40 million cubic feet of wet gas a day was stripped to 30 million cubic feet of dry gas, which was sold in lieu of tax.
"What you get is the condensate, which you can sell on the open market free of tax," Sandy said.
"You don't actually receive direct revenue for the gas, you receive indirect revenue by the fact you don't pay tax on the liquid sales," he said.
Sandy said Bukha provided Novus with benefits that would enable it to continue to expand.
The increased Bukha stakes followed an unsuccessful attempt earlier this year to snare the East Spar project in Western Australia from WMC Ltd, eventually acquired by rival Santos Ltd.
In the short-term, the substantial bid price would have been a weight on short-term cash flow, Sandy said.
But the Bukha deal, substantially less costly, varies in other ways too, he said.
"It is a good affect on cash flow and earnings in the short term, which will improve our earnings per share," Sandy said.
"Our philosophy is to use our cash engine to fund exploration to fund exploration," he said.
Sandy said a 10 percent stake served the company's purpose when it first floated its shares publicly in 1995 and was capitalised at A$150 million.
"But eventually it was time to make a decision, get bigger, or get out," Sandy said.
Sandy said Novus was open to new acquisitions, but said available properties were fetching premiums.
Particularly in Australia, where Novus holds 12.5 percent of the Harriet oil and gas field, quality assets are competitively sought after.
"Acquisitions of producing areas in Australia have become quite hot," he said.
Sandy said that while Australia offered new opportunities, Novus' main focus would remain on Asia.
Novus holds 25 percent of the Kakap production sharing contract, 26.03 percent of the Mallaca Strait project and 3.72 percent of the SE Sumatra contract.

Novus said he realised some analysts saw Novus as a potential takeover target, given its size and production and exploration base. "We have done absolutely nothing to take away a premium in that regard," he said.
Novus stock is held around 90 percent by institutions, with the largest stake being seven percent, he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
